# The Last Knowers

In the winter of 2008, in an apartment in Anchorage, Alaska, an eighty-nine-year-old woman died, and a language died with her. Her name was Marie Smith Jones, and she was the chief of the Eyak Nation and the last fully fluent speaker of Eyak, a language of the Alaskan coast. She had nine children, and none of them learned the language, because when they were young the world had made it very clear that Eyak was something to be ashamed of. So the words skipped a generation, and then there was nowhere left for them to go.

Late in her life, reporters asked her what it was like to be the last. She said it hurt, really hurt, and that she didn't know why it had to be her. Think about what her days contained. A language is meant to be spent — traded back and forth, spent on jokes and arguments and small talk. She had a fortune she could not spend. When she wanted to say something in Eyak, she said it to herself, or to the linguists who came with their recorders, or to no one.

By some estimates, a language falls silent about every two weeks. Of the roughly seven thousand languages still spoken on Earth, half may go quiet in this century. We hear these numbers so often they've gone flat, so it is worth slowing down and asking what, exactly, is lost.

A language is not a list of words. It is a way of paying attention. Grammar is frozen habit — the record of what a people, over centuries, found it necessary to notice. In Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Australia, there is no left or right. Directions are absolute: north, south, east, west. A speaker will tell you there's an ant on your southwest leg, or ask you to move your plate a little north-northeast, and to speak this way at all you must always know where north is — and the speakers do, effortlessly, a form of dead reckoning so constant it looks to outsiders like a sixth sense. In Tuyuca, spoken in the Amazon, you cannot make a bare statement. You must mark how you know: I saw it, I heard it, I deduced it, someone told me. Certainty wears its credentials on its sleeve. When such a language dies, we don't lose synonyms. We lose an instrument for dividing up the world, one that took ten thousand years of mornings to build.

The last speakers know this better than anyone. Their loneliness is of a very specific kind: they hold a key that opens a door no one else can see. In the Mexican village of Ayapa, the story went for years, the language Ayapaneco survived in exactly two old men — Manuel Segovia and Isidro Velazquez — who lived a few hundred meters apart and were not on speaking terms. The details were surely polished in the telling, but the image endures because it's the nightmare made literal: the last room left to a language, with two people in it, and the door between them closed.

Biologists have a word for the last member of a species: an *endling*. Martha, the last passenger pigeon, died in the Cincinnati Zoo on the first of September, 1914, in a species that had once darkened the sky for hours at a time — billions of birds, the most numerous on the continent, gone in a human lifetime. Lonesome George, the last Pinta Island tortoise, died in the Galápagos in 2012, and caretakers had spent years hoping, absurdly and touchingly, for eggs. What haunts me about endlings is that the moment of lastness is usually unwitnessed. Somewhere there was a day when the second-to-last passenger pigeon died, and Martha became the last, and nothing marked the transition. Lastness arrives silently, on an ordinary Tuesday.

Knowledge works the same way. It has a half-life, and nobody rings a bell when it expires.

Consider the lost techniques. The Byzantines had Greek fire — an incendiary weapon that burned on water and saved Constantinople more than once — and they guarded the formula as a state secret so successfully that it is now genuinely gone. Chemists can guess. No one knows. The Romans poured concrete of a quality we spent centuries unable to match; the Pantheon's dome, unreinforced, nearly nineteen centuries old, is still the largest of its kind on Earth, and for most of the time since it was built, no one alive could have built it. Only in the last few years have researchers reverse-engineered the recipe — volcanic ash, quicklime, seawater doing slow chemistry in the cracks — like codebreakers working a dead cipher.

Or take the Antikythera mechanism, hauled from a Greek shipwreck in 1901: a bronze device from the second century BC, gears within gears, that modeled the motions of the sky and predicted eclipses. Nothing of comparable mechanical sophistication appears anywhere in the record for a thousand years afterward. Somewhere a workshop closed. The master died; the apprentices scattered or never existed; the buyers stopped coming. And the world forgot that it had ever known how to do this. Forgot, even, to remember that it had forgotten.

Not all lost knowledge is ancient. It is often said that although the blueprints for the Saturn V rocket survive in full, we could not simply build another tomorrow — because the rocket was never only in the drawings. It was in the hands of the welders and the machinists, in tricks of eye and touch passed bench to bench, knowledge no one wrote down because no one thought it could be written down. The philosopher Michael Polanyi had a phrase for this: "We can know more than we can tell." You cannot learn to ride a bicycle from a book, and you cannot learn it by listening to a perfect description of bicycle physics. The knowing lives in the body. When the body goes, the knowing goes, unless it has been handed, hand to hand, to another body.

A technique dies with its last practitioner. A world dies with its last witness.

In February 2012, a woman named Florence Green died in England at the age of 110. She had served in the Women's Royal Air Force in 1918, and she was the last known living veteran of the First World War — a war that killed perhaps twenty million people. With her death, the Great War crossed over. It is now entirely a matter of record. No one alive remembers it. There is no one left to contradict the historians.

The strangeness is how recently the crossing happened — and how short the bridges are. In 1956, an elderly man named Samuel Seymour appeared on the American television show *I've Got a Secret*, and his secret was this: he had been at Ford's Theatre the night Abraham Lincoln was shot. He was five years old at the time. What he remembered was not the shot but a man tumbling from the balcony onto the stage, and his own childish fear for the falling man. The gap between a studio audience in the age of television and the Civil War is two long lives. We are closer to everything than we think — and then, in an instant, we are not. The last widows of Civil War soldiers, young women who had married ancient veterans during the Depression, lived into the twenty-first century, drawing pensions from a musket war in the age of the iPod. Then they, too, were gone.

The Malian writer Amadou Hampâté Bâ, speaking to UNESCO, said that in Africa, when an old person dies, a library burns down. He meant the oral traditions he spent his life recording. But the fire is general. Every death is a small Library of Alexandria, and most of the collection was never catalogued.

Which brings the matter home. You are, whether you know it or not, the last knower of certain things. You are the sole living repository of the exact smell of a particular kitchen on a particular holiday. You carry the precise sound of a laugh belonging to someone now gone — a laugh you would recognize in a crowd of ten thousand, and which no microphone ever captured. You are the only witness of small, unimportant, irreplaceable events: the way light came through a window in a house that has since been sold, the expression on a face in a moment no one else was watching. The vast majority of everything human beings have ever known has been like this — unrecorded, unrecordable, carried in bodies and lost with them. We are all walking archives with no backup, scheduled for demolition.

Write it down, we say. Record it. And we should; the alternative is worse. But it is worth being honest about what a recording saves. A tape gets the words; it does not get what the words were for. I can inherit a recipe, but not the hands. Linguists can record a last speaker for a thousand hours and preserve, in the end, a shadow of a knowing — the specimen, not the animal. The world's archives are full of these specimens, drawers and drives of them, and they are precious, and they are not the thing itself.

And yet — because this story is not only a dirge — there is the other direction. Knowledge dies, but it is also, constantly, being born, and sometimes, astonishingly, reborn.

Hebrew was for centuries a language of scripture and study, spoken natively by no one, until a household in Jerusalem raised a boy in the 1880s as the first native speaker of a resurrected tongue — and now millions argue about football in it. Cornish fell silent and now has speakers again, who learned it from books. In Massachusetts, the Wampanoag language had gone unspoken for some six generations when a social worker named Jessie Little Doe Baird began dreaming of her ancestors talking to her in words she could not understand. She went looking, and found that her language, remarkably, had left a paper trail — an entire Bible printed in 1663, along with deeds and letters, one of the largest written corpora of any Native American language. Working with linguists, she rebuilt it. She won a MacArthur grant. Her daughter became the first child in generations to grow up speaking Wampanoag. A language, it turns out, can sleep. And what sleeps can be woken.

Even Eyak. After Marie Smith Jones died in that Anchorage apartment, a teenager in Le Havre, France — a kid with no connection to Alaska at all — found the language online and taught it to himself from dictionaries and recordings, eventually flying to Alaska to help teach it to others. The last speaker was gone. A first speaker, of a strange new kind, had arrived. That is the hope tucked inside every story of lastness: the categories are not fixed. A last knower, with luck and stubbornness, can become a first one.

Knowledge, I've come to think, is not a stockpile. It is a relay race run in the dark, and the baton is always mid-pass — always at risk, always being fumbled, picked up, carried on. Most of what humanity knows exists at any moment inside some skull, warm and perishable, and the only storage technology we have ever had for the deepest things is the oldest one: find someone, and tell them. Show them. Let them stand at your elbow and watch.

You are carrying things no one else carries. Some of them deserve the pass. So tonight, while somewhere a last word is said into silence, somewhere else a first word will be said to a listening child — and the ledger, which is never closed, will balance a little differently. When you can, be on the first side of it. Say the thing. Teach the thing. The library is open late, and you are one of the librarians, and the fire is always closer than it looks.
